questions.q: Per this lesson's fast test, how do you tell the three data categories apart?
options: By checking which department's budget paid for the database server
By asking whether the record describes a thing (master), an allowed value (reference), or an event (transactional)
By checking the file format the data is stored in
By checking which programming language wrote the record
questions.explain: The lesson's test is conceptual: a customer is a thing (master), a country code is an allowed value (reference), and an order is an event (transactional).

questions.q: Which data category does this lesson describe as typically having the highest volume and the fastest rate of change?
options: Reference data
Master data
Transactional data
All three have identical volume and change rates
questions.explain: Transactional data is generated continuously by business activity (orders, payments, shipments), making it far higher volume and faster-changing than master or reference data.

questions.q: In the one-order-record example, what does the order's CurrencyCode field represent?
options: Master data, because currency is a core business entity
Reference data, because it is a standardized value like 'USD' that means the same thing on every order
Transactional data, because it changes every time the order updates
None of the three categories — currency codes are not data
questions.explain: CurrencyCode is a controlled, standardized code value — the defining trait of reference data — not a core entity or a timestamped event.

questions.q: What does this lesson say happens when reference data is governed as if it were master data?
options: Nothing changes; governance approach doesn't matter
It becomes more accurate automatically
It gets an overkill matching-and-stewardship workflow it doesn't actually need
The data is automatically deleted
questions.explain: The lesson gives the example of a twelve-value status code list receiving a full MDM-style matching and stewardship process, which is more process than that small, stable list requires.

questions.q: According to this lesson, who typically defines reference data, as opposed to master data?
options: Reference data is always invented ad hoc by individual employees
Reference data is usually defined by an external standard or a central internal authority, while master data is defined by the organization's own business entities
Reference data and master data are always defined by the exact same process
Neither master data nor reference data is ever formally defined
questions.explain: The lesson contrasts reference data (often from an external standard like ISO codes, or a central internal list) with master data (the organization's own core entities like its actual customers and products).
